Total $= 10^9 + 4 \times 10^8 = 1.4 \times 10^9$ cycles.

cse-2006-cs-47.approach: Kruskal adds edges in non-decreasing weight order (any order within ties), skipping cycle-forming edges. So a valid sequence must have non-decreasing weights. Check each option's weight sequence.

steps.title: Weight-1 edges
steps.body: a-b and d-f (in either order) are added first: components $\{a,b\}$, $\{d,f\}$.

steps.title: Weight-2 edges
steps.body: b-f joins $\{a,b\}$ with $\{d,f\}$; c-d brings in c. Both are accepted, in either order.

steps.title: Weight-3 edges

| Option | Weights in order | Valid? |

| B | 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 | yes |
| C | 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 | yes |
| D | 1, 1, 2, **3, 2** | no — d-e (3) before d-c (2) |

cse-2006-cs-48.approach: In a DFS tree of an undirected graph there are no cross edges: every non-tree edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors. A leaf has no descendants, so all its neighbours are ancestors on one root-to-leaf path.

steps.title: Neighbours of a leaf
steps.body: Let $u$ be a leaf. Every edge at $u$ is a tree edge to its parent or a back edge to an ancestor. So all neighbours of $u$ lie on the tree path from the root to $u$.

steps.title: Build the cycle
steps.body: Since $\deg(u) \ge 2$, $u$ has a back edge to some ancestor. Let $w$ be the **highest** (closest to root) neighbour of $u$. The tree path $w \to \dots \to \text{parent}(u) \to u$ plus the back edge $u\!-\!w$ is a cycle, and it passes through every vertex between $w$ and $u$ — hence through all neighbours of $u$. **Graph 2** (kills B): edges $r\!-\!x, x\!-\!u, u\!-\!r, x\!-\!y, y\!-\!v, v\!-\!r$. DFS $r \to x \to u$, then $x \to y \to v$: leaves $u, v$ of degree 2. Removing $r$ leaves $u\!-\!x\!-\!y\!-\!v$; removing $x$ or $y$ leaves $u\!-\!r\!-\!v$. No single vertex separates them, so (B) fails.

steps.title: Count misses
steps.body: Total elements $=512\times512=262144$. Sequential access misses once per block: $M_1=262144/16=16384$.

cse-2006-cs-81.approach: In P2 consecutive accesses are 4096 bytes apart, so each touches a new block, and the 512 blocks of one column map to only 8 cache lines — every access misses.

steps.title: Mapping of a column
steps.body: Lines $=32\text{K}/128=256$. One row $=512\times8=4096$ B $=32$ blocks. $A[j][i]$ lies in block $32j+\lfloor i/16\rfloor$, line $(32j+\lfloor i/16\rfloor)\bmod256$. As $j$ runs 0..511 the line takes only $256/32=8$ distinct values, each hit by 64 different blocks.

steps.title: Every access misses
steps.body: Before column $i$ is revisited (for $i+1$, same block), 63 other blocks have evicted it. So $M_2=262144$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Would need $M_2=131072$, i.e. half the accesses hitting.
Inverted ratio $M_2/M_1$.

cse-2006-cs-81.verification: A column needs 512 blocks but only 8 lines are available to it, so no reuse survives.

cse-2006-cs-82.approach: Build the shortest-path spanning tree from the root B1: pick each bridge's root port (lowest cost, ties to the lower port index), then one designated bridge per LAN (closest to root, ties to lower serial). Read the DFS order off the resulting bridge tree.

animation.caption: LANs named by their hosts; edge labels = port numbers

steps.title: Root and level-1 bridges
steps.body:
B1 has the least serial number: root, designated for LAN(H1,H2) and LAN(H3,H4).

B5 reaches the root in 1 hop through port 2 or port 3 → root port **2** (lower index). B3: ports 3 and 4 both 1 hop → root port **3**.

steps.title: Middle LANs
steps.body: LAN(H5,H6) can be served by B5 or B3 (both at distance 1); tie → lower serial **B3** (port 1). B5's ports 1 and 4 are blocked. LAN(H7,H8): only B3 is at distance 1 → **B3** (port 2).

steps.title: B4 and B2
steps.body:
B4: ports 1 and 2 both reach the root in 2 hops (via B3) → root port **1** (LAN H5,H6). B2: ports 1 and 2 both 2 hops → root port **1** (LAN H7,H8). Their other middle ports are blocked; each serves its own leaf LAN through port 3.

Bridge tree: B1 → {B5, B3}, B3 → {B4, B2}.

steps.title: Depth-first traversal
steps.body:
From B1 the child via port 1 (B5) comes first, then the subtree via port 2: B3, then B3's children B4 (port 1) and B2 (port 2).

DFS: **B1, B5, B3, B4, B2**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Tree B1 → (B5, B3), B3 → (B4, B2), visited depth-first.
Puts B5 under B3, but B5 attaches directly to B1.
Puts B2 under B5; B5 forwards to no middle LAN.
Visits B5 after B4, i.e. treats B5 as a descendant of B3.

pitfalls: Giving LAN(H5,H6) to B5 — B5 and B3 are equally close to the root, so the lower serial number (B3) wins.
cse-2006-cs-82.verification: Each LAN has exactly one designated bridge and each non-root bridge exactly one root port, so the result is a tree on all 5 bridges.

cse-2006-cs-84.approach: Split $i\ne j$ into $i>j$ ($a^+\,a^kb^k$) and $i<j$ ($a^kb^k\,b^+$). The grammar must force at least one extra $a$ or $b$ and must not allow $\varepsilon$ or equal counts.

steps.title: Grammar D
steps.body: $C\Rightarrow^* a^kb^k$, $A\Rightarrow^* a^p$ ($p\ge1$), $B\Rightarrow^* b^q$ ($q\ge1$). $AC=a^{p+k}b^k$ (more $a$'s), $CB=a^kb^{k+q}$ (more $b$'s). Together exactly $\{a^ib^j: i\ne j\}$.

steps.title: Counter-examples for the rest
steps.body:
A: $A\Rightarrow a$, $C\Rightarrow b$ gives $AC=ab$ ($i=j$).

B: $S\Rightarrow aS\Rightarrow ab$ ($i=j$).

C: $A,C\Rightarrow\varepsilon$ gives $\varepsilon$ ($i=j=0$).

optionAnalysis.reason: Derives $ab$ via $A\to a$, $C\to b$.
Derives $ab$ (any $a^ib^j$ with $i+j\ge1$).
Derives $\varepsilon$ and $ab$ ($A\to\varepsilon$, $C\to aCb\to ab$).
$A$ and $B$ add at least one unmatched symbol.

cse-2006-cs-84.verification: Generated short strings from D: a, b, aa, bb, aab, abb — none with equal counts.

cse-2006-cs-85.approach: Count rule applications in grammar D for $l>m$ (the case $l<m$ is symmetric): one $S$-step, $m$ uses of $C\to aCb$, one $C\to\varepsilon$, and $l-m$ steps for $A$.

steps.title: Case $l>m$
steps.body:
$S\to AC$: 1 step. $C\to aCb$ $m$ times then $C\to\varepsilon$: $m+1$ steps. $A$ must give $a^{l-m}$: $(l-m-1)$ times $A\to aA$ then $A\to a$: $l-m$ steps.

Total $=1+(m+1)+(l-m)=l+2$.

steps.title: Case $l<m$ and result
steps.body:
Symmetric with $S\to CB$: total $m+2$. Hence the length is $\max(l,m)+2$.

Check $a^2b$: $S\Rightarrow AC\Rightarrow AaCb\Rightarrow Aab\Rightarrow aab$ — 4 steps $=2+2$.
